top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) best meets the common criteria on achievement, maturity and attribution. It pairs a framework (the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium and task-based views of work) with transparent local-labour-market designs for import competition. The skill-premium line is about three decades old, the task framework over twenty years and the trade-shock papers over a decade. They have been replicated across countries and challenged on shift-share inference. That scrutiny has qualified the magnitude and persistence of the effects, not the existence of sizeable local adjustment costs. The citation can be worded around labour demand, wage structure and local adjustment, without claiming origination of the task framework or restating the 2023 and 2024 prizes. Attribution is the weak point. Dorn is excluded only by the three-name cap, and Katz's marginal credit, separate from his work with Goldin, is the most exposed. I cannot show from the supplied evidence that it is prize-sized. I therefore rank P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson), the cleaner single-discovery trade-shock version, a close second, and I would accept it if the committee cannot draft a single citation covering both strands. Both rank well above no award, because the work is mature, credibly identified and consequential.
recusal_note: No co-authorship, institutional or collaborator tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my profile. I disclose field proximity: I am an empirical labour economist using register data and quasi-experimental designs, and my class-size work is cited in the 2021 Scientific Background. That methodological affinity may bias me toward design-based evidence. As 2021 chair I gave the presentation speech, which reflected collective drafting and does not establish a preference. The ties other members disclosed are noted and not adjudicated.
